raw_findings.message: Items with no locations cause `reorderPoint` to divide by zero whenever a view is generated.
An SKU containing a newline is written directly into the movement log, allowing a request to forge additional log entries.
A GET to `/items` leaves `pathParts` with fewer than four elements, so indexing `pathParts[3]` panics and fails the request.
The handler reads the entire request body without a size limit, so a client can exhaust server memory with a sufficiently large body.
Malformed or empty JSON is silently accepted, allowing creation of a zero-valued item and returning success instead of rejecting the request.
A valid item with an omitted or null supplier makes `viewItem` panic when it dereferences `item.Supplier.Name`.
Negative movement quantities are not rejected, so reserve and release requests can reverse their intended stock and reservation effects; restock likewise accepts negative pack values.
Release does not check that the requested quantity is at most the reserved amount, allowing clients to make reservations negative and inflate stock.
Multiplying and adding attacker-controlled `int32` restock values can overflow and leave stock with an incorrect value.
A negative, oversized, or otherwise invalid `limit` can make the slice expression panic and fail the report request.
The unescaped `q` parameter is inserted into an HTML response, allowing an attacker to execute script in a viewer's browser.
The handler computes and sorts matches but writes only the query, so search requests never return the matching items.
The reset endpoint's administrator token is embedded in the source, so anyone who obtains the code can authenticate and erase the inventory.
The request log file is opened for every request and never closed, allowing repeated requests to exhaust the process's file descriptors.
`Get` returns a mutable item pointer after releasing the store lock, so concurrent handlers can race while reading or changing its fields and lose inventory updates.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The user-controlled SKU is written to the movement log without escaping, so a SKU containing a newline can forge movement-log entries.
The JSON decoder has no body-size limit, so a client can submit an extremely large item payload and exhaust server memory.
SKUs containing `/` are accepted here, but the item route rejects paths with an embedded slash, leaving those created items inaccessible by SKU.
Creating an item with an existing SKU silently replaces its stored item, allowing a request to erase existing stock and item data while returning a created response.
The reserve, release, restock, and reset handlers do not restrict methods, so requests using methods such as GET can perform state-changing operations.
Releasing reserved stock can overflow `Stock` when restocking has raised it near `MaxInt32`, wrapping the resulting stock to a negative value.
The reset handler accepts any HTTP method, so an authorized request using GET or another unintended method can reset the inventory.
The request path is written to the audit log without escaping, so a path containing an encoded newline can forge additional log entries.

raw_findings.message: An item with no locations makes `reorderPoint` divide by zero, causing item views and reports to panic.
A GET request to `/items` leaves `pathParts` with fewer than four elements, so indexing element 3 panics and terminates that request.
`io.ReadAll` accepts an unbounded body, so a client can send a very large `/items` request and exhaust server memory.
Malformed or overflowing JSON is accepted because the unmarshal error is ignored, allowing invalid or partially decoded items to be inserted or overwrite an existing SKU.
Creating an item with an omitted or null supplier leaves `item.Supplier` nil, and viewing that item dereferences it and panics.
A negative reserve quantity passes the stock check and then increases stock while decreasing reserved inventory, allowing callers to manipulate inventory totals.
A release quantity greater than the reserved amount is accepted, making reserved inventory negative and adding unreserved units to stock.
Untrusted pack values are multiplied and added using `int32` without range checks, so large values can overflow and corrupt stock totals.
An attacker-controlled limit is used directly as a slice bound, so a negative value or a value greater than the item count panics the report handler.
The search query is written directly into an HTML response, so a query containing markup or script is reflected as executable content.
The reset endpoint's admin token is hardcoded in the source, so anyone who obtains the code can authenticate to reset the inventory.
The audit log is opened for every request but never closed, so repeated requests exhaust the process's file descriptors.
`Get` returns a mutable item pointer after releasing the lock, so concurrent handlers can race while reading and updating inventory and lose updates.

The reset token is a fixed credential embedded in the source, allowing anyone who obtains the code to authorize a reset request.
auditRequests opens requests.log for every request but never closes the file, allowing repeated requests to exhaust the process's file descriptors.
